teaser.text: General Dynamics builds military equipment and government technology systems, alongside Gulfstream private jets and the services that keep them flying. Its business is a chain: customers fund ships, vehicles, software and aircraft; General Dynamics pays people and suppliers to deliver them, then keeps what remains after operating costs.

blocks.heading: Where could General Dynamics's shares go?

paragraphs.text: GD’s weighted forecast reaches $351.85 in October 2027 and $381.13 in October 2029, hinging on Gulfstream deliveries, shipyard throughput and cash conversion. Management promises $55,700 million of 2026 revenue and diluted EPS of $16.80–$16.90. It expects 160 Gulfstream deliveries, a 14.7% Aerospace margin and a 7.4% Marine Systems margin. Free cash flow conversion is expected at about 105%, although second-half cash will be lighter amid investment, pensions, taxes and use of prior advances.

The weighted prices imply a 6% return including dividends at the first date and a 19% return at the last. Scenario probabilities are 25% bear, 57% base and 18% bull. The October 30, 2026 earnings call tests Marine milestones, Gulfstream deliveries and heavier second-half cash demands. By October 2027–2028, supplier flow and earned hours must improve shipyard throughput without margin pressure. By October 2028–2029, funded backlog must become sales and free cash flow. The investment rests on turning production progress and backlog into cash without sacrificing margins.

blocks.heading: How much cash does General Dynamics really make?

paragraphs.text: Operating cash exceeded net income, and free cash flow represented about 94% of earnings after capital spending. That is useful, but stock compensation preserves cash while imposing a cost on shareholders, so a stricter measure deducts it.

Because 76% of revenue was recognized over time in 2024, these timing gaps matter. A large Spanish collection coincided with repayment of an advance, while tax changes improved payment timing. By July 2026, net unbilled receivables had risen to $9,255 million from $8,380 million at year-end, showing why reported revenue and collected cash must be checked together.

blocks.heading: What do investors pay for General Dynamics?

paragraphs.text: The price-to-earnings ratio, or P/E, says how much investors pay for each dollar of earnings per share. A trailing P/E uses the last twelve months; a forward P/E uses the next twelve months. The lower forward multiple implies expected earnings growth if the share price does not change. But GD’s earnings include estimates. Contract-cost revisions added $0.46 to diluted EPS in 2025, and a revised estimate of the cost to finish a vehicle contract can change reported profit before the customer pays anything new.

blocks.heading: What has General Dynamics guided for 2026?

paragraphs.text: The improvement does not depend on promising many more Gulfstream aircraft. The annual delivery target remains unchanged, so GD must earn better economics from the aircraft and submarines it delivers. Management has raised its 2026 EPS outlook twice; the test is whether the increases reflect repeatable gains such as fewer labor hours and more reliable suppliers.

blocks.heading: Did General Dynamics keep its past promises?

paragraphs.text: The results support the awards more convincingly than general praise. GD forecast diluted earnings per share of US$14.75–14.85 in January 2025 and delivered US$15.45. Three-year return on invested capital reached 13.2% against a 12.6% goal, producing a performance-unit payout of 128% of target.

blocks.heading: What do General Dynamics' last eight quarters show?

paragraphs.text: Revenue and operating income both rose from the comparable quarter, while gross and operating margins expanded. Net income and diluted EPS also increased, so the improvement was not merely a function of selling more products.

blocks.heading: What should I watch in General Dynamics' next results?

paragraphs.text: The October 30 earnings call should show whether improved production survives the heavier second-half demands on cash.

Marine revenue could moderate because materials received earlier are being installed later. That would not automatically mean production weakened; the evidence should be construction milestones, installation progress, margins and cash conversion.
